title: Section 267 — Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

content.overview: BNS s. 267 — Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding. BNS restatement of IPC 228. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 228. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 267 is the rule on “Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding”. The section provides that whoever, intentionally offers any insult, or causes any interruption to any public servant, while such public servant is sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 267 exists so that “Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding” has a closed legal test in Chapter XIV — Of False Evidence and Offences Against Public Justice. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Perjury, screening, harbouring, false charge, and failing to appear on a bond.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 267 constitutes a key component of Chapter XIV (Of False Evidence and Offences against Public Justice) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, addressing intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding. The provision balances personal liberty with public interest and social order. The prosecution must establish every statutory element beyond reasonable doubt: the specified actus reus, the requisite mens rea, and any relevant statutory circumstances. Modern judicial interpretation emphasizes substantive fairness, proportionality in sentencing, and adherence to constitutional safeguards. Where statutory exceptions or provisos are attached to the section, the accused must establish facts bringing the case within such provisions under evidentiary standards.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 267 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: Section 267 vs General Attempt: Section 267 penalizes the substantive conduct specified in Chapter XIV; inchoate attempts without specific provisions fall under the general attempt provisions.

Section 267 vs Cognate Chapter Offences: Liability under Section 267 is distinguished by its specific mental threshold and the particular legal interest protected under Of False Evidence and Offences against Public Justice.

Rule: Under BNS s. 267, liability attaches upon proof of the statutory actus reus accompanied by the requisite mens rea without lawful justification.
